title: GRIFFITH - Godlike Confidence & Devilish Charisma (Berserk analysis)
summary: A narrated character essay on Griffith from Berserk: his predator-like beauty, his 'do as you will' philosophy (really 'do as I will'), his unshakable self-belief and his charisma. He argues Griffith's godlike conviction is both his strength and his fatal flaw, and that his followers serve as means to his dream of a kingdom.
claims: Griffith's beauty hides a predator: the grace of a bird of prey with a taste for battle
Griffith's 'do as you please' drops the 'as long as you hurt no one' half; for his men it really means 'do as I will', freedom put to the service of his dream
Most people stop at thinking or saying what they want and never act; Griffith turns every desire into reality, including winning people
His self-belief rests on instinct, not physical power or status; he isn't the strongest or fastest but his sword never misses
Fanatical devotion to himself is his greatest strength and also his worst flaw, since no defeat can be allowed to touch his image
Popularity is subconsciously convincing people that following you benefits them; we are drawn to people we see as superior
A god never asks 'can I?', it says 'I will'; the common man who doubts himself follows the one who seems guided by fate
His dream of a kingdom means he will tolerate no equal and everyone else becomes a means to that end
Nothing is more dangerous than a tyrant unaware of where he is leading his followers
